title: Monday at 09:00 for 2,400 people
scenario:
You are head of operations at a logistics company with 3,000 staff, 2,400 of them in offices. A 60-person pilot of a shipping-document assistant ended with a clear go. The assistant calls the Claude API.

The CEO wants every office worker on it next Monday at 09:00. Finance asks you for a plan. The exhibit shows the draft.
exhibit:
Shipping-document assistant: rollout DRAFT (made-up example data)

Pilot result
  60 users, 6 weeks. Go rule: at least 85% of drafts accepted.
  Result: 91% accepted. Pilot token cost: $450 a month.

Draft plan
  Launch    Mon 09:00: all 2,400 office staff switched on.
  Testing   Testers and staff share the workspace "docs-prod"
            and one API key.
  Budget    Organization monthly spend limit: $30,000.
            Plan: set the docs-prod limit to $40,000 "for headroom".
            Pilot cost x 40 (2,400 / 60) = expected $18,000 a month.
  Fallback  The manual process is retired on launch day.
  Training  One announcement email.

questions.prompt: The tool calls an API. What does OpenAI's rate limits page warn about switching 2,400 people on at 09:00?

options.text: Nothing, because staying inside the rate limits means that no errors can happen at all.
options.explanation: The page says a slow_down error can occur even when traffic is within its per-minute limits.

options.text: A fast jump in traffic can return slow_down errors even inside limits, so start teams in steps.
options.explanation: Right. The page says slow_down can occur within the limits, and gives a rule of thumb for ramping. A wave plan also adds gates and stop rules.

options.text: Only the price changes at high traffic, so the main risk is a much bigger monthly bill.
options.explanation: The page warns about errors from a fast ramp. Cost is a separate matter, covered by spend limits.

options.text: A higher limit always fixes it, so ask the vendor for more capacity before the launch.
options.explanation: A higher limit does not remove the ramp-rate rule. The error is about how fast traffic rises.

questions.prompt: Testers and staff share one workspace and key. Which fix fits Anthropic's workspace guidance?

options.text: Create development, staging and production workspaces, with testers in the first two.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's workspaces page suggests this split, with lower rate limits for development and full limits with monitoring for production.

options.text: Keep one shared workspace, and ask the testers to run their scripts only at night.
options.explanation: A test script gone wrong can still use the production budget and rate limits at any hour.

options.text: Give testers their own personal accounts at the vendor, outside the company's control.
options.explanation: The company would lose control of keys, limits and data terms. The fix is separate workspaces inside the organization.

options.text: Let testers keep using the production key, with a note that says it is for tests.
options.explanation: A note changes no setting. Test traffic still counts toward production limits and cost.

questions.prompt: The draft sets the docs-prod spend limit to $40,000. What is the best change?

options.text: Keep $40,000. The extra headroom costs nothing unless somebody actually uses it.
options.explanation: Anthropic's page says workspace limits can't be higher than the organization's. The $30,000 organization limit applies anyway.

options.text: Remove the workspace limit, because the organization limit already protects all of it.
options.explanation: The organization limit protects the total, but one workspace could still use all of it. Workspace limits and alerts catch problems earlier.

options.text: Set it to $30,000, so the workspace can use the whole organization budget if needed.
options.explanation: That allows this one tool to use the entire company budget. Other workspaces could be blocked.

options.text: Set it below $30,000, near the $18,000 estimate, with alerts at set thresholds.
options.explanation: Right. Workspace limits can be at or below the organization's, and the page says to configure alerts at thresholds.

questions.prompt: The draft retires the manual process on launch day. What should the rollback plan say instead?

options.text: State that no rollback is needed, because the pilot reached 91% accepted drafts.
options.explanation: A pilot of 60 people does not show how 2,400 people will use the tool. The plan still needs a way back.

options.text: Name a trigger, an action and an owner, and keep the manual process for some weeks.
options.explanation: Right. A way back needs an exact trigger, a way to stop the tool, and a fallback so work does not stop.

options.text: Plan to retrain staff if anything goes wrong, since the tool itself will be fine.
options.explanation: That assumes the problem is always people. A serious incident may need the tool to stop.

options.text: Keep the manual process only for the pilot group, and retire it for all others.
options.explanation: The people most affected by a problem, the new users, would have no fallback.
